module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 383

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/383](https://www.erdosproblems.com/383)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos383

/--
Is it true that for every $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that the largest prime
divisor of
$$
  \prod_{i = 0}^k (p ^ 2 + i)
$$
is $p$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_383 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ k, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Nat.maxPrimeFac (∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 0 k, (p ^ 2 + i)) = p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos383

review.notes:
The single declaration Erdos383.erdos_383 matches the current erdosproblems.com statement term by term. The quantifiers are in the right order (∀ k, then infinitely many p). The product range is `Finset.Icc 0 k` = {0,…,k}, matching \prod_{0≤i≤k}, with base p². `Nat.maxPrimeFac … = p` states "the largest prime divisor is p", and the yes/no `answer(sorry)` slot comes before all quantifiers.

Lean experiments (scratch files in /workspace/review):
(1) I proved that for prime p the product is greater than 1, so the junk values of `maxPrimeFac` at 0 and 1 are never reached.
(2) I proved the k = 0 instance: the product is p², so every prime qualifies. This does not change the ∀-statement, and the source's own "for every k" with ∏_{0≤i≤k} includes k = 0 anyway.
(3) #eval on small cases: for k = 1 the primes that work are 7, 41, 43, 47, …; for k = 2, 41, 157, …
(4) I checked the forum's witness p = 9188057 with the Lean definitions. The largest prime factors of p²+i are below p for i = 1..10, and p²+11 has the prime factor 1407006523921 > p. This matches the forum's factorizations exactly.

On the primary source [ErGr80], which I could not access: for prime p > k, p does not divide p²+i when 1 ≤ i ≤ k. So the Lean condition is equivalent to "all prime factors of ∏_{1≤i≤k}(p²+i) are less than (or at most) p". Excluding the finitely many p ≤ k does not affect infiniteness. Any such alternative wording in the book therefore gives the same problem.

Status: `research open` is correct. erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (accessed 2026-09-23), and the teorth database says open. The only proof claim describes itself as partial (exponent 2−1/(2k)+ε, not 1).
